## Chapter 5: Mixture of Experts: More Parameters, Selective Compute {#sec-ch5}

*Total, Active, Compute, and Communication Are Four Different Questions*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Distinguish a dense feed-forward block from a sparse MoE block, and
  explain the roles of the router, experts, top-$k$ selection, routing
  weights, and an optional shared expert.
- Calculate total and active parameters for the routed-expert bank
  *and* for the complete model, and explain why these are not the same
  ratio.
- Explain why sparse activation does not make unused expert weights
  disappear from memory, and describe load imbalance, expert capacity,
  and what a load-balancing loss penalizes (without guaranteeing
  balance).
- Distinguish MoE sparsity (which *parameters* activate) from sparse
  attention (Chapter 4's which *positions* are scored), and explain why
  expert parallelism introduces device-to-device communication.
- Compare model capacity, computation, memory footprint, and
  communication as four separate quantities.

### Why this matters

Every mechanism so far has changed *how* a fixed set of parameters is
used per token. MoE changes *which* parameters get used at all.
Getting this chapter's central distinction wrong -- treating "fewer
active parameters" as "fewer stored parameters," or as "proportionally
less compute," or as "no communication cost" -- is the single most
common MoE misreading, and this chapter is built to prevent exactly
that.

### Visual overview

![MoE replaces the feed-forward sublayer, not attention: a router
selects a subset of experts per token; unselected experts are stored
but not used for that
token.](figures/rendered/fig-dense-vs-moe.svg){#fig-dense-vs-moe}

### Technical core

**From dense to sparse.** Chapter 2's gated feed-forward block sends
every token through the *same* parameters. A sparse MoE layer replaces
that single block with a **router** that scores $E$ **routed experts**,
selects the top-$k$ for each token, runs only those experts, and
**combines** their outputs with routing weights before returning the
result to the residual stream. Exact routing/combination rules vary by
architecture; this chapter's formulation is representative, not
universal.

**Routing.** For a token representation $x$:

$$
r = W_r x, \qquad p = \text{softmax}(r), \qquad T(x) = \text{TopK}(p, k)
$$ {#eq-router}

$r$ are the router logits, $p$ the per-expert probabilities, and $T(x)$
the selected top-$k$ index set. The combined output is:

$$
y(x) = \sum_{e \in T(x)} \alpha_e(x) \cdot \text{Expert}_e(x)
$$ {#eq-moe-combine}

with $\alpha_e(x)$ a routing weight (often, but not always, the
normalized $p_e$). Not every production MoE normalizes weights, handles
capacity, or adds auxiliary losses identically.

**Total vs. active parameters.** With $p_e$ parameters per routed
expert, an optional always-active shared-expert path of $p_s$
parameters, and $p_{\text{base}}$ for everything else (attention,
embeddings, norms, the router):

$$
\underbrace{E \, p_e}_{\text{routed total}}, \quad
\underbrace{k \, p_e}_{\text{routed active}}, \qquad
\underbrace{p_{\text{base}} + E p_e + p_s}_{\text{model total}}, \quad
\underbrace{p_{\text{base}} + k p_e + p_s}_{\text{model active}}
$$ {#eq-total-active}

$E/k$ is the routed-expert-bank's *own* ratio -- it is **not** the
complete model's total/active ratio, since $p_{\text{base}}$ and $p_s$
are active regardless of routing. Published "A-B" model notation
(e.g. "236B-21B") is convention-dependent; check official
documentation before assuming what it counts. Active parameters are
also not identical to exact FLOP counts (the router itself costs
compute too).

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"A 64-expert top-2 MoE activates only 2/64 of the whole model."** It
does not, unless the statement is explicitly restricted to the routed
expert bank. Attention, embeddings, normalization, the router, and any
shared expert stay active regardless -- @eq-total-active's model-level
ratio is always closer to 1 than $E/k$ is.
:::

![For one token, only $k$ of $E$ routed experts are active; base
parameters and any shared expert are active regardless; all $E$
experts remain stored either
way.](figures/rendered/fig-moe-total-vs-active.svg){#fig-moe-total-vs-active}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"Inactive experts consume no memory."** They do. An expert not
selected for a given token is still a stored weight matrix that must
fit in memory -- sparsity is about *compute*, not *storage*.
:::

**Load balancing and capacity.** Without constraints, many tokens may
route to a few popular experts, overloading them while others sit
idle -- wasting capacity and risking *routing collapse* (reduced
specialization). Systems bound this with a **capacity factor** (how
many tokens an expert can take before **overflow**, handled by
dropping or rerouting, implementation-dependent) and an **auxiliary
load-balancing loss** that *encourages*, but does not *guarantee*,
balanced routing in any given batch.

**Shared experts.** Some transformations are useful for most tokens;
an always-active shared expert can capture that shared knowledge,
reducing pressure on routed experts to duplicate it -- DeepSeekMoE
adds shared experts while *reducing* routed top-$k$ activation to hold
total active compute roughly constant ([@src-36]). Shared experts are
not universally necessary; their benefit depends on architecture and
training.

**Expert parallelism.** Routed experts may be split across devices, so
tokens must be dispatched to whichever device holds their selected
expert and results returned -- an **all-to-all** exchange, in plain
terms: every device may need to send tokens to, and receive results
from, every other device. Uneven routing produces uneven device
workloads, and this communication can offset the sparse-compute
benefit MoE is chasing. Fewer active expert parameters does **not**
mean all expert weights fit on one device -- total storage and active
computation answer different questions. (Collective-communication
algorithms and cluster topology are out of scope here.)

![Tokens dispatch to whichever device holds their selected expert;
routing can be imbalanced (E1 here gets 3 of 6 tokens), and results
must return to their originating
token.](figures/rendered/fig-moe-routing-parallelism.svg){#fig-moe-routing-parallelism}

### Worked example

**Parameters.** $E=8$, $k=2$, $p_e = p_s = 100\text{M}$,
$p_{\text{base}} = 1.2\text{B}$ (verified programmatically; see the
Build and Version Note):

| Quantity | Total | Active | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Routed expert bank | 800M | 200M | 4.0 ($=E/k$) |
| Complete model | 2.1B | 1.5B | 1.4 |

: $E/k=4$, but the complete model's ratio is 1.4 -- $p_{\text{base}}$ and $p_s$ stay active either way {#tbl-moe-params-worked}

**Routing imbalance.** 6 tokens, top-1, 4 experts (matching
@fig-moe-routing-parallelism): assignment $\{E_1{:}3, E_2{:}1,
E_3{:}1, E_4{:}1\}$ against a nominal balanced load of 1.5/expert. At
capacity factor 1.2 (capacity $=2$ per expert, verified
programmatically), $E_1$ overflows by 1 token. Neither this ratio nor
this overflow count is a universal law -- both depend on the specific
config and routing outcome, not stated here as one.

### Compare and contrast

| | Dense FFN | Routed MoE | MoE + shared expert |
|---|---|---|---|
| Expert paths/token | 1 (always) | $k$ of $E$ | $k$ of $E$, plus 1 shared |
| Total parameters | smallest | largest | largest |
| Active parameters | equals total | $\ll$ total (bank-level) | $\ll$ total (bank-level) |
| Routing required? | no | yes | yes |
| Load-balancing concern | none | yes | yes |
| Distributed communication | none extra | all-to-all (if expert-parallel) | all-to-all (if expert-parallel) |
| Principal benefit | simplicity | more capacity, compute roughly held | also reduces routed redundancy |
| Principal complication | none | routing, imbalance, communication | also costs always-active compute |

: MoE does not automatically mean lower latency, lower memory, better quality, or balanced routing -- each row is a tradeoff {#tbl-moe-comparison}

### Applied exercise

A serving team must choose between a dense model and a MoE model with
the same *active* parameter count. Using this chapter's total/active
distinction (not benchmark numbers), predict which has the larger
serving memory footprint, and state the one architectural fact that
makes your answer certain regardless of which specific models are
compared.

### Interview lens

*"A model has 64 experts and activates 2 per token. Explain what that
tells you -- and what it does not tell you -- about parameters, FLOPs,
memory, and communication."* A strong answer states that it tells you
the *routed-expert-bank's* activation ratio (2/64), but not the whole
model's total/active ratio (base and shared-expert parameters are
unaffected), not exact FLOPs (routing and combination cost something
too), not memory footprint (all 64 experts must still be stored), and
not communication cost (which depends on how routing lands across
devices, not on $k$ or $E$ alone).

### Chapter recap

- MoE replaces the feed-forward sublayer with a router, top-$k$
  selected experts, and a weighted combination -- attention is
  unchanged.
- $E/k$ is the routed-expert-bank's own total/active ratio, not the
  complete model's -- base and shared-expert parameters stay active
  regardless of routing.
- Inactive experts are still stored; sparsity changes compute, not
  memory footprint.
- Load-balancing losses encourage, but do not guarantee, balanced
  routing; capacity factors and overflow handling are
  implementation-dependent.
- Shared experts trade always-active compute for reduced redundancy
  across routed experts -- not a universal requirement.
- Expert parallelism's all-to-all communication is an unavoidable
  architectural consequence once experts are distributed, and can
  offset the sparse-compute benefit.
- Model capacity, computation, memory footprint, and communication are
  four separate quantities -- no single number answers all four.

### Sources and further reading

Primary sources: [@src-28] (sparsely-gated MoE and its top-$k$ routing
and load-balancing losses), [@src-29] (top-2 gating, its auxiliary
load-balancing loss, and expert-parallel sharding), [@src-30] (top-1
routing and a different load-balancing loss form -- these formulations
are genuinely not equivalent, not restated here as one "the" loss),
[@src-36] (DeepSeekMoE's shared-expert motivation and compute
tradeoff, verified against the paper's full text, not a snippet).
Secondary/supporting: [@src-14]. Detailed distributed-training
implementation, collective-communication algorithms, kernel
optimization, inference-engine configuration, expert quantization,
model-specific benchmark comparisons, post-training, and a survey of
routing research are all out of scope for this chapter.
